podcast.title: Hip-Pocket Records Releases (1966)
podcast.body: Roulette Records was among the labels that released singles on Hip-Pocket Records in 1966, collaborating with Filco and Ford. These inexpensive, bendable plastic discs were sold for $0.69 at Ford dealerships and Woolworth stores, featuring artists such as Ben Morrison. `"They got Atlantic, Mercury, and Roulette records to release singles this way, selling them for $0.69 at four dealerships and through Woolworth stores."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Hugo and Luigi's Co-ownership
podcast.body: Roulette was a new label set up by Morris Levy, George Goldner, and Alan Freed. Goldner and Freed quickly dropped out, but Hugo and Luigi ended up with a 50% stake in the label, producing numerous hits and their own instrumental tracks. "Morris Levy, who was setting up a new label, Roulette, with George Goldner and Alan Freed."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Morris Levy's Exploitative Label
podcast.body: Roulette Records was established by Morris Levy, known for his mafia connections and predatory business practices. Along with his publishing company, Patricia Music, Roulette served as a primary vehicle for Levy to exploit the intellectual property of young, often Black, artists. "Levy then formed a publishing company, Patricia Music, and a record label, Roulette, and started into the business of properly exploiting young black people."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 35: "Why Do Fools Fall In Love?" by Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers

podcast.title: Morris Levy's Involvement in Twist Craze
podcast.body: Upon the surge in popularity of "The Twist," Morris Levy, associated with Roulette Records, quickly moved to capitalize on the craze. He signed Joey D and the Starlighters to his label and brought in Henry Glover to produce their twist song. "Morris Levy sprang into action. Levy wanted a piece of this new twist thing, and since he didn't have Chubby Checker, he was going to get the next best thing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Morris Levy's Unfair Practices
podcast.body: When Hugo and Luigi were recruited by RCA, Morris Levy, the owner of Roulette, released them from their contract only on the condition that they relinquish their shares in Roulette for a price "far less than they were worth." "Morris Levy let them go, so long as they gave up their shares in Roulette, for far less than they were worth."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
